note.explanation: For complete equilibrium, the forces must balance in both directions and the turning effects must balance too. This means the object has no acceleration and no rotation.
examples: A picture hanging still has balanced upward tensions and downward weight.
Two equal and opposite forces along different lines can have zero resultant force but still turn a body.
note.checkAnswer: The vector sum of all external forces is zero, and the vector sum of all torques about any point is zero.
note.simple: An object is completely in equilibrium when it neither speeds up or slows down nor starts turning.
note.checkQuestion: What three sums must be zero for a body to be in complete equilibrium?
note.title: Conditions of Equilibrium
steps: Choose the object you are studying and show the forces acting on it.
Choose x- and y-axes that make resolving forces as easy as possible.
Resolve forces into components if needed.
If needed, use Στ = 0 and solve the equations.

options: ΣF_x = 0 and ΣF_y = 0 only
Στ = 0 only
ΣF_x = 0, ΣF_y = 0, and Στ = 0
ΣF_x = 0 and Στ ≠ 0
mcqs.stem: Which set of conditions must be satisfied for a body to be in complete equilibrium?
rationales: These two force conditions alone do not rule out a turning effect.
Zero net torque alone does not rule out a non-zero resultant force.
All force components and the net torque must be zero for complete equilibrium.
A non-zero net torque means the body can rotate, so it is not in complete equilibrium.

options: Only the weight of the body
The vector sum of all external forces
The largest force acting on the body
The force acting through its centre
mcqs.stem: According to the first condition of equilibrium, what must be zero?
rationales: The weight need not be zero; it can be balanced by other forces.
The first condition requires the vector sum of all external forces to be zero.
The largest individual force need not be zero or cancelled by one force alone.
A force through the centre is not the general statement of the first condition.

options: ΣF_x = 0
ΣF_y = 0
Στ = 0
ΣF_x = 0 and ΣF_y = 0
mcqs.stem: Which equation expresses the second condition of equilibrium?
rationales: This is the force-balance condition along the x-axis.
This is the force-balance condition along the y-axis.
The second condition requires the vector sum of torques to be zero.
These two equations express the first condition, not the second.

options: It must be treated together with every other object
It should be treated separately
Only its weight should be shown
The forces it exerts on its environment must be included
mcqs.stem: When applying the conditions of equilibrium, how should each selected object be treated?
rationales: The textbook method selects objects and treats each one separately.
This is the stated method: each object should be treated separately.
The diagram should show all forces acting on the object, not just its weight.
The diagram includes forces acting on the object, not forces it exerts on its environment.

options: Choose axes that make as many forces as possible lie along the axes
Always choose the axes horizontally and vertically
Choose axes so that every force is diagonal
Choose axes only after solving the equations
mcqs.stem: How should axes be chosen to simplify an equilibrium problem?
rationales: This reduces the number of forces that need to be resolved into components.
Horizontal and vertical axes are not always the most convenient choice.
Making every force diagonal would usually increase the number of components needed.
Axes are chosen before resolving forces and applying the equations.

options: The forces have different magnitudes
The forces have equal magnitudes and opposite directions
The forces act along the same line of action
The body has no weight
mcqs.stem: Two equal and opposite forces can have zero resultant force but still turn a body when:
rationales: Different magnitudes generally give a non-zero resultant force.
With separated lines of action, equal and opposite forces can form a couple and produce torque.
Forces along the same line of action do not form the separated-force couple described.
A body's weight does not determine whether the pair of forces produces torque.

options: Translational equilibrium only
Rotational equilibrium only
Complete equilibrium
Neither force nor rotational equilibrium
mcqs.stem: A body has ΣF_x = 0 and ΣF_y = 0, but Στ is not zero. What is true?
rationales: The resultant force is zero, so the first condition is satisfied.
A non-zero sum of torques means rotational equilibrium is not satisfied.
Complete equilibrium requires the torque sum to be zero as well.
The force conditions are satisfied, so it is not correct to say there is no force equilibrium.

options: The centre of gravity is at the highest position
The upward forces equal the downward forces and the torque sum is zero
Every force on the body is zero
The body has no mass
mcqs.stem: A picture hangs at rest from two strings. Which statement describes its equilibrium?
rationales: This is not a condition for equilibrium.
At rest, its forces and torques balance; these are the equilibrium conditions.
Individual forces can be non-zero while their vector sum is zero.
A hanging picture has mass; its weight is balanced by the strings.

rubric.why: The vertical force balance is needed to relate the tensions to the weight.
rubric.how: Use ΣF_y = 0 to write T_1 + T_2 − 5 N = 0.

rubric.why: The torque equation determines one tension using the given distances.
rubric.description: Apply the torque condition about B.
rubric.how: Set the clockwise and anticlockwise torques equal about point B.

rubric.why: Both tension values are required for the complete answer.
rubric.how: Substitute T_1 = 2.5 N into the force equation and give both tensions with units.

modelAnswer: Since, there is no horizontal force, so Σ F_x = 0
Apply Σ τ = 0, selecting point B as point of rotation.
putting the values, 5 N × 0.2 m − T_1 × 0.4 m = 0
Putting the value of T_1 and w in the force equation, 2.5 N + T_2 − 5 N = 0

written.text: State and explain two conditions of equilibrium.
written.finalAnswer: First condition: ΣF_x = 0 and ΣF_y = 0. Second condition: Στ = 0.

rubric.why: The first condition explains translational equilibrium.
rubric.description: State and explain the first condition.
rubric.how: Explain that the vector sum of external forces is zero, or give its x- and y-component equations.

rubric.why: The second condition rules out rotation.
rubric.description: State and explain the second condition.
rubric.how: Explain that the vector sum of torques about any point is zero.

modelAnswer: First condition of equilibrium: A body is in translational equilibrium only if the vector sum of all the external forces acting on it is equal to zero.
For coplanar forces, this means ΣF_x = 0 and ΣF_y = 0.
Second condition of equilibrium: The vector sum of all the torques acting on a body about any point must be zero.
Mathematically, Στ = 0; this is the condition for rotational equilibrium.

written.text: Why an accelerated body cannot be considered in equilibrium?
written.finalAnswer: An accelerated body has a non-zero resultant force, so ΣF ≠ 0; it does not satisfy the first condition of equilibrium.

rubric.why: Acceleration shows the body is not in translational equilibrium.
rubric.description: Connect acceleration to the resultant force.
rubric.how: Use Newton’s second law, F = ma.

rubric.why: Equilibrium requires the vector sum of forces to be zero.
rubric.how: Explain that a non-zero resultant force means the first condition of equilibrium is not satisfied.

modelAnswer: By Newton’s second law of motion, F = ma.
For an accelerated body, a ≠ 0, therefore the net force F is not zero.
But the first condition of equilibrium requires ΣF = 0.
Therefore, an accelerated body cannot be considered in equilibrium.

rubric.why: The vertical force balance connects the tensions to the weight.
The torque balance uses the equal distances from the centre.

rubric.how: Use zero net torque and the 2 m and 4 m distances.

rubric.why: The question asks for the tension in each wire.
rubric.how: Use the force equation to find the second tension and state the pair.

modelAnswer: Since the signboard is in equilibrium, ΣF_y = 0.
Apply Στ = 0, selecting one wire as the point of rotation.
The weight acts 2 m from the selected wire and the other tension acts 4 m from it.
Putting T_1 = 100 N in Eq. (i), 100 N + T_2 − 200 N = 0

rubric.why: The vertical component of tension balances the ball's weight.
The horizontal component of tension balances the applied force.
rubric.how: Write F = T cos 60° and calculate F.
Give F = 2.9 N and T = 5.8 N.

modelAnswer: The ball is in equilibrium, so ΣF_y = 0.

examTips: A board paper may ask you to state or explain the two conditions of equilibrium; write the force condition and the torque condition separately.
For numerical questions, marks are commonly awarded for writing the correct equilibrium equation, substituting the values, and giving the final answer with units.
Choose a point for the torque equation that makes an unknown force pass through it; that force then produces zero torque about that point.
Show the direction or sign of each force or torque consistently. Do not claim complete equilibrium if you have checked only the forces or only the torques.

Use the torque condition about one wire; the weight is 2 m from that wire and the other wire is 4 m away.

example.question: A picture is suspended by means of two vertical strings as shown in Fig. 4.21. The weight of the picture is 5 N, and it is acting at its centre of gravity. Find the tension T_1 & T_2 in the two strings.

explain.title: First condition: forces balance
explain.body: By Newton’s second law of motion, F = ma. If a body is in translational equilibrium, then a = 0, therefore, net force F should be 0 or ΣF = 0. A body is said to be in translational equilibrium only if the vector sum of all the external forces acting on it is equal to zero. For coplanar forces, ΣF_x = 0 and ΣF_y = 0.

explain.title: Second condition: torques balance
explain.body: The second condition of equilibrium implies to the rotational equilibrium which means that the body should not rotate under the action of the forces. The vector sum of all the torques acting on a body about any point must be zero. Mathematically, Στ = 0.

explain.title: Complete equilibrium
explain.body: A body will be in complete equilibrium when ΣF_x = 0, ΣF_y = 0, and Στ = 0. The first two equations prevent a resultant force; the last prevents a resultant turning effect.

explain.title: A useful problem-solving order
explain.body: Treat each object separately, draw the forces acting on it, choose convenient axes, resolve forces when needed, and apply the force equations. If necessary, apply the torque equation and solve the equations together.

mistakes: Writing ΣF = 0 and assuming the body must be completely in equilibrium without checking Στ = 0.
Forgetting to split a slanting force into x- and y-components.
Including forces that the object exerts on its environment instead of showing only forces acting on the object.
Using a torque distance that is not the perpendicular distance from the selected point of rotation.
Dropping units or using inconsistent signs in the torque equation.
